w: Gum surgeries sit on a scale. A simple extraction may need no cut and no flap at all. A graft over a receded root needs a small flap lifted just a little. A sinus lift or ridge graft needs a big flap opened with several cuts. Which cut and flap to use is partly a matter of the surgeon's preference (Dr. Basma said two surgeons can disagree on the same case), but a small set of designs covers almost everything. Naming an incision: it's about the tooth, not the technique The most-missed point in this session: intrasulcular and crestal are the same cut. Only the name changes, depending on whether a tooth is there. With a tooth present, the blade goes into the sulcus (the small gap between gum and tooth) and separates the gum fibers from the tooth all the way around: cheek side, tongue side, and through the papillae (the gum points between teeth). That is intrasulcular. Where there is no tooth, there's no sulcus, so the same straight cut along the top of the ridge is called crestal. Including more teeth in this cut gives a bigger flap and more room to work, but including teeth you don't need hurts the look of the result for no gain. When that cut alone doesn't open enough room (most big bone grafts), you add a vertical releasing incision at the line angle of a tooth (the corner where the front surface turns into the side surface). It opens a bigger flap without adding more teeth to the horizontal cut. One vertical plus an intrasulcular cut across three teeth (for example, distal of #7 with the sulcus cut on 7, 8 and 9) makes a triangle-shaped pyramidal flap, which is enough for an implant with a small bone graft on top. Two verticals, one on each side, make a trapezoidal flap. That is needed for large vertical bone grafts, because two releases let the flap slide up and close over the graft without tension. One vertical usually can't stretch that far without tearing. One more design barely lifts anything: the envelope (pouch) flap. The papillae are never touched. Only the cheek-side gum is loosened, just enough to slide it up over a gum graft (from the patient or a donor), leaving the gum between the teeth completely intact. It is the go-to design for covering exposed roots, where disturbing the papilla would work against the cosmetic goal. Reading a flap design Besides how it is opened, a flap is described three more ways. Thickness: full-thickness lifts the periosteum (the thin skin over the bone) with the flap and bares the bone; split-thickness leaves the periosteum on the bone. Where it goes back: moved up past the CEJ to cover roots, or moved down for crown lengthening and bone reshaping. Papilla: kept intact or not. A sulcular flap (sulcus cut only, no vertical) gives the least room and is hard to move because the tissue stays attached at the sides. It is the smallest option, used for small grafts or a single implant. Adding one more tooth on each side (still no vertical) buys a bit more room without a releasing cut. Full vs. split has a simple rule: if the surgery involves bone in any way, go full thickness and expose it. If it's only about soft tissue, go split thickness and leave the periosteum behind as a living bed. That covers every case in the course. Implants, bone, ridge and sinus grafts, crown lengthening and bone reshaping are all full thickness. Gum grafting is the one split-thickness exception, because the graft needs that blood-rich bed to connect its blood vessels to the patient's. A fourth incision: sub-marginal, for eliminating a pocket The in-class review added a fourth cut that works differently from the others: the sub-marginal incision. "Sub" means below: it is made below the gum edge, not in the sulcus or on the ridge. The other cuts are for access and get closed back where they were. This one removes tissue on purpose: it is scalloped through the pocket wall and the gum above it is cut away, not lifted and put back. The goal is getting rid of a deep pocket during bone surgery. If a site probes 6 mm where 3 mm is normal, trimming about 3 mm of pocket wall leaves a shallow, cleanable sulcus instead of a deep pocket that keeps refilling with bacteria between visits. The catch is deliberate: this cut creates recession (the gum edge ends up lower on the tooth after healing). That is the right trade when the alternative is a pocket the patient can't keep clean. It is the wrong call, and never done, on a site being treated for recession. The question is always what the real problem is: a deep pocket calls for a sub-marginal cut; thin or receded gum calls for a graft. They aren't contradictory, just answers to different problems. Choosing a suture material Stitches come in two big groups. Absorbable ones dissolve in the body on their own (gut, chromic gut, and synthetics like Vicryl and Monocryl). Non-absorbable ones have to be taken out, usually at 10-14 days, or are left long-term (silk, ePTFE, polypropylene/Prolene, nylon). Plain gut dissolves fastest (7-10 days). Chromic gut is treated with chromium salts and lasts a bit longer (10-14 days). Synthetics like Vicryl keep their strength for 2-3 weeks and dissolve over a longer time. Absorbables make sense for quick cases in kids or simple extractions, where a removal visit is a hassle. Non-absorbables like ePTFE are preferred over big bone grafts because they attract less plaque, are strong, and won't break down too early. The course chart compares six materials by natural vs. synthetic, single-strand vs. braided, how fast they dissolve, strength, how much they irritate tissue, and how they handle (full chart in Review). Chromic gut: natural, single strand, dissolves fastest (7-10 days), handles very badly. Used at extraction sites, implants without extra grafting, or to hold a collagen membrane. The two synthetic dissolvers differ by build. PGA is braided, dissolves slowest (55-70 days), handles beautifully, but irritates tissue, which fits ridge and sinus grafts that heal slowly. PGCL is a single strand, dissolves faster (22-55 days) and is gentler on tissue, which fits gum grafts and cosmetic crown lengthening. Of the ones that must be removed: polypropylene behaves like nylon and doesn't stick to tissue; silk handles beautifully but irritates tissue the most of anything on the list and comes out at 7 days; PTFE costs the most and is used for nearly every surgery except pure gum grafts. Single strand vs. braided isn't just about feel; it's about infection. A braided stitch soaks up and traps bacteria like a wick. A smooth single strand doesn't. That is exactly why silk scores so badly for irritation. If you use a braided stitch, wipe it with chlorhexidine gauze before pulling it out, so you don't drag plaque back through the wound. Grafting from the palate: donor-site selection and protection Keratinized gum (pale pink, firm, doesn't move) protects the tooth from the wear of chewing, the way tough skin protects you in a fall better than the thin lining inside your cheek. Non-keratinized tissue (red, thin, loose, full of blood vessels) can't take that load. When a tooth or implant doesn't have enough firm gum, you graft some, and the palate is the best source because it is all firm, keratinized, fixed tissue. Take it from the molar area, not the premolar area. The premolar area has more fat under the surface, and fat melts away after it is moved, so a graft with too much fat visibly shrinks. From the surface down, the palate is: epithelium (surface layer), then connective tissue (lamina propria), then fat over bone. A connective tissue graft keeps only the middle layer: the surface is trimmed off and the fat is avoided on purpose. Grafts work because two raw, cut surfaces held together will join their blood vessels and heal as one, the same way two cut fingers held together can reattach, but two fingers just pressed together (skin intact) never will. That's also why the site receiving the graft is prepared split thickness: the periosteum left on the bone gives the graft a living surface to fuse to. The donor spot on the roof of the mouth is left as an open wound, and it hurts (compared in class to a bad pizza burn, since every sip and swallow touches raw nerve endings). Options to protect it: a composite stent made before the harvest to keep the palate's shape, PRF (a gel made from the patient's own blood) laid over the wound, or a custom palatal stent or night guard worn for at least three days while it heals over, taken out only to clean. Watch out for the greater palatine artery in this area; nicking it is the most common cause of serious bleeding during a palatal harvest. The needle matters as much as the thread. A reverse cutting needle keeps its flat side toward the tissue as it comes up, so it is less likely to tear through than a regular cutting needle. A more curved needle takes a deeper bite. A thicker needle goes through more tissue but needs more wrist turn. For thread size, a bigger number means a thinner thread, and thinner thread needs more knots to hold. Choosing a technique Single interrupted stitches (and the figure-8 version) are the everyday default: each one is tied on its own. Horizontal mattress stitches are a must for bigger bone grafts and keep the flap edges from rolling inward, but tied too tight they choke the blood supply to the edge and can cause bone death and the wound opening up. Vertical mattress stitches pull tissue together most closely and turn the edges out; they are the choice for rebuilding papillae in the front of the mouth or closing an opening into the sinus. Continuous and continuous-locking stitches put the bites close together for a tight seal, but if one throw fails the whole line can come loose (a real risk with slippery single-strand thread), so they're kept for long toothless areas, bone smoothing and root-tip surgery. Sling and periosteal-anchor stitches finish the list: one wraps around a single tooth to reposition a flap, the other anchors the flap to the periosteum to hold it lower or to the side. Five surgical principles Every cut and flap in the course follows five rules: (1) one firm, continuous stroke, not several shaky ones; (2) keep the cut away from the actual defect, never right over it; (3) put vertical cuts at the line angle of the tooth; (4) lift the periosteum as part of the flap; and (5) make the base of the flap at least as wide as its free edge, because once the flap is lifted, the base is its only blood supply. Ortho heads-up: if an orthodontist plans to push thin-gummed front teeth further forward, graft first to thicken the gum. Pushing a tooth through thin bone and gum tends to cause recession, and it's easier to prevent than to fix. The best time to treat recession is always as early as possible.
